title: Rollout Pass-Rate Control: Steering Binary-Reward RL Toward Its Most Informative Regime

paper.title: Rollout Pass-Rate Control: Steering Binary-Reward RL Toward Its Most Informative Regime
paper.abstract: Abstract SWE-bench-style agentic reinforcement learning relies on expensive stateful trajectories, yet substantial compute is wasted on sampled rollout groups with skewed pass rates, where binary rewards provide a weak contrastive signal. We frame this inefficiency as a pass-rate control problem and show that a 50% pass rate is the most informative operating point: it maximizes reward entropy, the probability of surviving group filtering, RLOO advantage energy under GRPO, and success–failure contrastive structure. Guided by this principle, we propose Prefix Sampling (PS), which replays trajectory prefixes to steer skewed groups toward this regime: successful prefixes serve as head starts for mostly failing groups, while failing prefixes serve as handicaps for mostly passing groups. In stateful agent environments, prefix states are reconstructed through replay while replayed tokens are excluded from the loss, restricting optimization to continuations generated by the current policy. On SWE-bench-style agentic RL, PS delivers end-to-end wall-clock speedups of 2.01 × 2.01\times on Qwen3-14B and 1.55 × 1.55\times on Qwen3-32B while preserving or improving final verified performance. For 14B, the SWE-bench Verified peak rises from the baseline peak of 0.273 0.273 to 0.295 0.295 under PS. Additional mathematical reasoning experiments on AIME 2025 show the same pass-rate control pattern and decompose the gains into replay, bidirectional coverage, and adaptive control.

Additional mathematical reasoning experiments on AIME 2025 show the same pass-rate control pattern and decompose the gains into replay, bidirectional coverage, and adaptive control. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is now widely used for post-training on tasks with clear external feedback, including software engineering and mathematical reasoning [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Within this paradigm, online policy-gradient methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) rely on rollout trajectories to produce contrastive learning signal [ 1 ] . As these tasks move toward agentic reinforcement learning, rollouts become longer, more interactive, and substantially more expensive to generate [ 3 , 4 ] . This raises a basic efficiency question: when rollouts dominate compute and wall-clock time, how much of that effort actually produces useful learning signal? Existing filtering heuristics show that not all rollouts are equally valuable, but the relationship among rollout pass rates, compute, and training benefit remains under-specified. To reduce compute spent on uninformative rollouts, many RLVR pipelines use group-level filtering [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . We use group filtering to denote the GRPO-style practice of discarding rollout groups whose binary rewards are all zero or all one. This operation is sometimes called rejection sampling in RLVR implementations, but differs from positive-only rejection sampling, which keeps only successful samples for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement. The need for such filtering is implicit in DeepSeekMath/GRPO, since group-relative normalization gives no relative advantage signal when every reward in a group is identical [ 1 ] . DAPO later formalizes this exclusion as dynamic sampling, replacing all-zero/all-one groups until the batch is filled [ 2 ] . Beyond filtering, prior work injects guidance, reallocates rollout budget, mixes supervision, or calibrates hint strength to rescue difficult instances or preserve effective batches [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . These methods reshape pass rates implicitly. They rarely derive the target regime from binary-reward learning signal, and they do not directly control both too-hard and too-easy groups under fixed compute. We therefore formulate Rollout Pass-Rate Control (Rollout-PRC) for binary-reward RLVR tasks such as software engineering and mathematical reasoning [ 10 , 11 ] . For a task with multiple rollouts, the rollout pass rate is the fraction of successful rollouts in the group. Even after group filtering, many retained rollout groups in SWE-bench-style tasks remain highly skewed, such as 1 / 8 1/8 or 7 / 8 7/8 , and provide weak contrast. Three perspectives—reward entropy, RLOO advantage energy under GRPO, and success–failure contrastive structure—all identify the same target: training is most informative when rollout pass rates are close to 50% [ 12 , 1 , 13 ] . Rollout-PRC turns pass-rate management from an implicit byproduct of training into an explicit control objective. Guided by Rollout-PRC, we propose Prefix Sampling (PS), a bidirectional framework that routes skewed rollout groups toward the 50% regime through trajectory prefix replay. For mostly failing groups, it replays a successful prefix as a head start; for mostly passing groups, it replays a failing prefix as a handicap. Unlike hint-based approaches that rely on oracle solutions or reasoning traces from stronger models [ 5 , 6 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] , Prefix Sampling reuses trajectories produced by the current policy itself. In stateful agent environments, it reconstructs the prefix state through the existing rollout path and masks replayed tokens from the loss, so optimization is restricted to fresh continuations generated by the current policy. On SWE-bench-style agentic RL, it reaches the baseline’s best verified score in up to 1.76 × 1.76\times fewer evaluation steps and delivers 2.01 × 2.01\times and 1.55 × 1.55\times end-to-end speedups on Qwen3-14B [ 18 ] and Qwen3-32B [ 19 ] without sacrificing final performance. Our contributions are: • We identify Rollout Pass-Rate Control (Rollout-PRC) as a principled efficiency objective for binary-reward RL, and show that a 50% rollout pass rate maximizes reward entropy, RLOO advantage energy under GRPO, and success–failure contrastive structure. • We propose Prefix Sampling, a bidirectional pass-rate steering framework that replays trajectory prefixes to move skewed rollout groups toward this high-signal regime. The method works in stateful multi-turn agent environments because it reconstructs prefix state through the existing rollout path, applies optimization only to the continuation generated by the current policy, and adjusts prefix length for different pass-count buckets. • We demonstrate cross-scale gains on SWE-bench-style agentic RL and AIME 2025 reasoning [ 20 ] , including up to 1.76 × 1.76\times fewer benchmark-evaluation steps, 2.01 × 2.01\times end-to-end speedup, and mechanistic and ablation evidence showing that the gains stem from steering rerollout pass rates toward the 50% target. 2 Method Figure 1 : Prefix Sampling pipeline. For each task we sample a rollout group and route it by pass count: degenerate 0 / 8 0/8 or 8 / 8 8/8 groups are filtered, already balanced 3 / 8 3/8 – 5 / 8 5/8 groups are used for standard training, and skewed groups provide replay prefixes. Mostly failing hard buckets reuse a successful prefix as a head start, while mostly passing easy buckets reuse a failing prefix as a handicap. The current policy generates fresh continuations from the replay-reconstructed prefix state; masking applies RL loss only to continuation tokens, steering rerollouts toward 50 % 50\% without crediting replayed actions. Counts in the diagram are schematic; experiments use N = 8 N=8 rollouts. 2.1 Why target 50% rollout pass rate Given the limitations of implicit filtering, a natural question is which rollout pass rate yields the strongest binary-reward learning signal.
